Real-world observational cohorts rarely arrive clean: you may have skewed predictors, clinic clusters, survey sampling weights, selective dropout, and preferred `tidymodels` feature engineering pipelines. `tidytmle` lets you plug in custom `recipes`, `parsnip` model specifications, `workflows`, and `workflowsets::workflow_set` ensembles directly—while enforcing causal hygiene automatically.

> **Why cross-fitting and Super Learning matter here:** Combining diverse algorithms inside a cross-validated Super Learner lowers the chance of functional-form misspecification, while out-of-fold predictions keep standard errors honest without classical Donsker smoothness restrictions (Zheng & van der Laan, 2011).

## Role-Aware Recipe Splitting & `workflow_set` Super Learning

A subtle bug in DIY causal ML code is leaking treatment assignment `a` or cluster IDs (`clinic_id`) into the propensity model `g(W)` when reusing a single `recipe(y ~ ., data = df)`. `tidytmle` clones and adapts your recipe per nuisance role (`Q`, `g`, and `C`) so `a` stays in `Q(A, W)` and `C(A, W)` while strictly blocked from `g(W)`'s predictors:

```{r level2, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7.8, fig.height = 5.4, fig.alt = "Paired horizontal bar chart showing Super Learner ensemble weights alongside cross-validated error for Outcome (Q), Treatment (g), and Missingness (C)"}
library(tidytmle)
library(recipes)
library(parsnip)
library(workflowsets)

df <- sim_causal_cohort(
  n = 350,
  outcome_type = "continuous",
  censoring_rate = 0.15,
  n_clusters = 15L,
  seed = 101
)

base_rec <- recipe(y ~ ., data = df) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

q_models <- list(
  glm = linear_reg() |> set_engine("glm")
)
if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)) {
  q_models$enet <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.05, mixture = 0.5) |> set_engine("glmnet")
} else {
  q_models$lm <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm")
}

q_wf_set <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(base = base_rec),
  models = q_models
)

g_spec <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm")

fit_l2 <- tmle_spec(
  outcome    = y,
  treatment  = a,
  covariates = c(age, sex, starts_with("lab_")),
  censoring  = delta,
  id         = clinic_id,
  estimand   = "ate"
) |>
  set_preprocessing(base_rec) |>
  set_outcome_learners(q_wf_set) |>
  set_treatment_learners(g_spec) |>
  set_resamples(v_folds = 5L) |>
  fit(data = df)

fit_l2
autoplot(fit_l2, type = "learners")
```

## Selective Dropout (`NA` Outcomes), Cluster SEs & Survey Weights

Dropping patients whose follow-up outcomes are missing (`NA`) creates **selection bias** whenever sicker participants drop out more often. When `outcome` contains `NA`s and `censoring` is omitted, `tidytmle` automatically introduces $\Delta = \mathbb{I}(\neg\text{is.na}(Y))$, models informative missingness $C(A, W) = P(\Delta = 1 \mid A, W)$, and folds inverse-observation weights directly into the Clever Covariate.

> **Key Identifying Assumption — Missing At Random (MAR):** Inverse-probability censoring weights remove dropout bias provided outcome observation depends only on measured baseline covariates and treatment ($\Delta \perp Y(a) \mid A = a, W$, with positive observation probability $C(a, W) > 0$). If dropout depends on the *unobserved* outcome itself even after conditioning on $(A, W)$ (*Missing Not At Random*, MNAR), sensitivity analyses are required.

Native `hardhat::importance_weights()` and `hardhat::frequency_weights()` are likewise carried cleanly through both nuisance workflows and cluster-robust standard errors:

```{r missingness, fig.alt = "Dumbbell plot comparing confounder imbalance before and after IPW/TMLE weighting"}
df_miss <- dplyr::select(df, -delta)
df_miss$survey_wt <- hardhat::importance_weights(runif(nrow(df_miss), 0.7, 1.5))

fit_auto_c <- tmle_spec(
  outcome    = y,
  treatment  = a,
  covariates = c(age, sex, starts_with("lab_")),
  id         = clinic_id,
  weights    = survey_wt
) |>
  set_resamples(v_folds = 5L) |>
  fit(data = df_miss)

check_tmle(fit_auto_c)
autoplot(fit_auto_c, type = "balance")
```

Notice how confounding imbalance drops cleanly into the green `< 0.10` balanced band—ready to generate paper prose via `report_tmle(fit_auto_c)`.

## Stratified Outcome Modeling, Fluctuation Submodels & Outer-Fold Super Learning

Three methodological controls give you finer-grained command when datasets have strong effect modification, severe positivity stress, or strict parity requirements:

* **Pooled (`stratify = FALSE`) vs. Arm-Stratified `Q` (`stratify = TRUE`):** By default, `tidytmle` fits a pooled Super Learner $\bar{Q}(A, W)$ enriched with treatment-interaction workflows (`glmnet_interact`), natural splines (`glmnet_spline`), and `ranger(..., always.split.variables = treatment_col)`. When treatment-effect heterogeneity is complex or sample size per arm is large, `set_outcome_learners("default", stratify = TRUE)` fits separate Super Learners on treated and control arms (T-learner mode) while retaining joint TMLE targeting.
* **Weighted (`"logistic"`) vs. Covariate (`"logistic_covariate"`) Fluctuation:** The default `"logistic"` submodel fits arm-specific weighted-intercept fluctuations (`target.gwt = TRUE`), avoiding logit-scale boundary explosions under skewed propensity weights. Classical two-parameter clever-covariate fluctuation (`target.gwt = FALSE`) is available anytime via `set_targeting(fluctuation = "logistic_covariate")` or `retarget(fit, fluctuation = "logistic_covariate")`.
* **Outer-Fold Simplex FISTA Stacking:** Each candidate workflow is fit exclusively out-of-fold across the `rsample` splits, and convex simplex ensemble weights ($w_k \ge 0, \sum w_k = 1$) are solved over the concatenated out-of-fold risk matrix using FISTA—avoiding nested $V \times 10$ inner cross-validation loops while keeping predictions honest.
